description: Hi! I’m a Computer Science student majoring in Data Analytics. I enjoy working with data, exploring new ideas and learning new technologies. I’m excited to challenge myself through NASA Space Apps Challenge and put my skills into practice while gaining new experiences.
summary:
After the Mission is an interactive website that works like a digital space museum. It tells the stories of six NASA machines that stayed behind after their missions: Apollo 11’s Eagle and Surveyor 3 on the Moon, Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars, and Pioneer 10 in deep space.

Each machine “tells” its own story in five chapters, from launch to legacy. The creative first-person narration is labelled “Imagined voice” and kept visibly separate from “Mission record” panels of verified facts from NASA sources. Visitors can filter explorers by destination, step through an interactive timeline for each mission, and test themselves with a 12-question quiz that gives instant feedback.

This answers the challenge by turning dense mission archives into accessible, accurate stories for students and casual space fans. It also corrects a common misconception: not every machine is “abandoned”. Some were left behind on purpose, and one is still travelling. Understanding these machines shows how each mission made the next one possible, and inspires the next generation of explorers.
details:
What it does and how it works
After the Mission is an interactive website that works like a digital space museum. It tells the stories of six NASA machines that stayed behind after their missions: Apollo 11’s lunar module Eagle and Surveyor 3 on the Moon, Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars, and Pioneer 10 in deep space.

  • Home: a “Where they are now” list gives each machine’s current location and status.
  • Explore: visitors filter the machines by the Moon, Mars or Deep Space.
  • Story pages: each machine tells its story in five chapters (My beginning, My mission, What I discovered, My final days, My legacy). Every story has fact callouts and an interactive mission timeline.
  • Legacy page: connects the missions, showing how each one answered a question that made the next possible.
  • Quiz: 12 questions with instant feedback, the correct answer and a score.
  • Sources page: lists every reference and image credit.

Benefits
NASA’s mission information is accurate but often technical. This project makes it accessible to school students and casual space fans without losing accuracy. It also corrects a common misconception: not all equipment is “abandoned”. Each machine’s real status is explained. Some were left on purpose, some lost power, Ingenuity is grounded but was programmed to keep logging data, and Pioneer 10 is still travelling.

Intended impact
I want young people to see space machines as explorers with histories, not just hardware, and to understand that today’s missions build on these earlier ones. I hope it sparks curiosity about science, engineering and space careers.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks, backend or database.
  • Data: all content lives in one data file, so adding a new explorer updates the cards, filters, stories and sources automatically.
  • Development and hosting: built in Visual Studio Code, version-controlled with Git and hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Images: authentic NASA images, loaded from Wikimedia Commons.
  • Research: NASA mission pages, NASA/JPL news releases and the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA).

Creativity
Each machine narrates its own journey in the first person, which gives it a personality and makes the history memorable. To protect accuracy, every chapter visibly separates the “Imagined voice” from the verified “Mission record”, and the narration never invents events, conversations or discoveries. The design is a cinematic space-museum look, with an animated starfield and colour-coding for each destination.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy: dates and statuses were checked against official sources, launch, landing and end-of-mission dates were kept separate, and anything unconfirmed is stated as uncertain.
  • Accessibility: readable fonts, good contrast, keyboard navigation, support for reduced-motion settings, and layouts that work on phones.
  • Simplicity: a structure that is easy to maintain and to expand with more explorers.
  • Credit and copyright: proper credits for all images.
